hook_text: One pair of points. Five answers. The most predictable topic in maths — if you know the moves.
clip_script: Analytical geometry cannot surprise you, and here's why: it only knows five moves, and they all start from two points. Take P at minus three, one, and Q at five, minus five. Move one, distance: eight across, six down, and Pythagoras flies the diagonal — sixty-four plus thirty-six is a hundred, root it, ten. Move two, midpoint: average both coordinates — one, minus two. Move three, gradient: minus six over eight, minus three quarters — downhill to the right. Move four, the equation: you already have m, so substitute one point and c falls out. Then the secret weapon nobody uses: push the unused point through your equation. If it lands, your whole answer is certified — ten seconds, marks protected. Move five, inclination: gradient equals tan of the angle. Falling line? Take the size, inverse tan gives thirty-six comma eight seven, subtract from one eighty — one forty-three comma one three degrees. Never hand the calculator's negative angle to a marker. Five moves. One pair of points rehearses all of them. That's the entire topic — and that's why the strongest students love it: it pays the same marks every single time.
visual_style: A city grid lighting up block by block as a crow cuts the diagonal; five glowing move-cards stacking up one by one; a final checkmark stamping down as the unused point lands on the line.
mood: Confident and demystifying — a cheat-sheet energy, secrets handed over.
pacing: Rapid-fire through the five moves with a beat of pause on the unused-point check, then a punchy close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make the five moves automatic.
